questions.prompt: Why does std::variant<NonDefault, int> fail to default-construct, and what standard helper fixes it?
questions.code:
struct NonDefault { explicit NonDefault(int) {} };
std::variant<NonDefault, int> v;
options: std::variant default-constructs its first alternative (NonDefault); placing std::monostate first makes the variant default-constructible
std::variant requires every alternative to be default-constructible
std::variant always starts empty like std::optional
std::variant selects int automatically when the first alternative lacks a default constructor
questions.explanation: A default-constructed std::variant constructs its zero-indexed alternative. If the first type is not default-constructible, std::variant's default constructor is deleted; putting std::monostate as the first alternative provides a lightweight empty initial state.

questions.prompt: Why does storing a lambda that captures std::unique_ptr<int> fail with std::function<int()> but succeed with std::move_only_function<int()>?
questions.code:
auto p = std::make_unique<int>(7);
std::move_only_function<int()> f = [p = std::move(p)] { return *p; };
options: std::function cannot store lambdas with captures at all
std::function requires stored callables to be CopyConstructible, whereas std::move_only_function requires only MoveConstructible
std::move_only_function stores pointers without calling destructors
std::function only works with function pointers
questions.explanation: std::function mandates CopyConstructible targets because std::function itself is copyable. C++23 std::move_only_function drops copyability, enabling move-only captures such as std::unique_ptr.

questions.prompt: What happens when calling f() through const std::function<int()>& vs const std::move_only_function<int()>& wrapping a mutable lambda?
questions.code:
const std::function<int()> a = [n = 0]() mutable { return ++n; };
const std::move_only_function<int()> b = [n = 0]() mutable { return ++n; };
options: Both fail to compile because calling a mutable lambda through const is ill-formed
Both compile and increment n on every call
a compiles and mutates n despite being const; b fails to compile because std::move_only_function<int()> does not declare a const operator()
b compiles while a throws std::bad_function_call
questions.explanation: std::function::operator() is always const-qualified regardless of the wrapped callable, silently allowing mutation through a const std::function. std::move_only_function honors qualifiers in its signature: const invocations require std::move_only_function<int() const>.

questions.prompt: Why does std::vformat(fmt, std::make_format_args(42)) fail to compile under C++20/23 after DR P2905R2?
questions.code:
std::string fmt = "{}";
auto s = std::vformat(fmt, std::make_format_args(42));
options: std::vformat does not accept integers
std::format_args only accepts std::string arguments
std::make_format_args returns void
std::make_format_args takes Args&... (lvalue references) to prevent storing dangling pointers to temporaries inside format_args
questions.explanation: Defect report P2905R2 changed std::make_format_args from forwarding references (Args&&...) to lvalue references (Args&...) so callers cannot accidentally bind temporaries like 42 or std::string{} whose lifetime ends before std::vformat runs.

questions.prompt: Under what circumstance can std::variant::valueless_by_exception() become true?
options: Whenever a variant holds std::monostate
When an exception is thrown during type-changing assignment or emplace() after the previous alternative was destroyed and before the new one finishes constructing
Whenever a variant is moved from
Whenever std::get<T> fails with std::bad_variant_access
questions.explanation: According to [variant.status], a variant never becomes valueless during normal construction or moves; it becomes valueless_by_exception() only if an exception interrupts a type-changing assignment or emplace() between destroying the old value and constructing the replacement.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes invoking an empty std::move_only_function from invoking an empty std::function?
options: Calling an empty std::move_only_function is undefined behavior, whereas calling an empty std::function throws std::bad_function_call
Both throw std::bad_function_call
Calling an empty std::move_only_function returns a default-constructed R{}
std::move_only_function cannot be default-constructed or empty
questions.explanation: Under [func.wrap.move.inv], invoking an empty std::move_only_function has a precondition that *this is non-empty (undefined behavior if violated), avoiding the branch and exception path mandated by std::function in [func.wrap.func.inv].
